newsitem.title: USA: Banks tighten U.S. consumer lending - Fed.
newsitem.headline: Banks tighten U.S. consumer lending - Fed.

text.p: Banks are tightening standards for making consumer loans and imposing stricter limits on credit cards, according to a survey of senior loan officers issued on Monday by the Federal Reserve.
By contrast, lending standards for business loans were little changed overall, the survey of lending officers at 55 large domestic banks and 23 foreign-owned banks found.
In fact, a significant number of banks were making it easier to qualify for commercial and industrial loans than was the case when the last survey was issued late in May.
Banks were more wary about issuing credit cards because of a rise in sudden bankruptcies.
About half the banks that use a credit-scoring model to decide who qualifies for a credit card said they had tightened the cutoff scores needed to qualify for a card.

"Many banks are charging off consumer loans at a higher-than-expected rate given the delinquency rate on these loans at their bank," the survey reported. "These banks attribute this development largely to a rise in bankruptcies with a shorter than usualintervening period of delinquency."

All in all, the survey concluded, "banks are pulling back somewhat in their lending to consumers." Nearly a third of banks have lowered their credit limits on new or existing credit card accounts and half tightened standards for approving credit card applications.

But on the business side, there was little change from May in requirements set for loans. "A few banks ... eased standards for loans to large corporations but standards for smaller firms were essentially unchanged," the survey said.
Ten to 20 percent of bankers said demand for commercial and industrial loans was up, mostly from smaller businesses.
"However, demand for home mortgages was reportedly weaker at many banks," the Fed survey said.

Both the May and the August surveys have shown banks less eager to make consumer loans, apparently fearful that they won't be repaid and that consumers are more likely than in the past to abruptly declare bankruptcy.
"These results represent the first time since 1981 that two consecutive surveys have shown a net reduction in willingness to make consumer loans," the Federal Reserve said.
